lead: One transistor stage gives gain in the tens. A microphone or sensor often needs hundreds or thousands. Chaining stages multiplies gain, and the coupling between stages decides what else changes: DC level, bandwidth and impedance. RC coupling uses a capacitor, transformer coupling uses a coil, and direct coupling uses a wire. The same choice appears in audio preamps, radio receivers and op-amp internal circuits.
prereq: You need: 2.5 and 2.6 for single-stage gain, input resistance and output resistance.

sections.h3: RC coupling: a capacitor between stages

blocks.text: A coupling capacitor CC sits between the collector of one stage and the base of the next. The capacitor blocks DC, so each stage keeps its own bias point from 2.2. For the AC signal, CC is almost a short at midband. The signal passes, and the voltage gain of the two stages multiplies.

items: Input resistance of the next stage and C<sub>C</sub> form a high-pass corner. Below it, gain falls.
Output resistance of the first stage and input resistance of the second form a divider. This divider lowers gain unless the second stage has high input resistance.
RC coupling is cheap, small and wideband. Audio preamps and low-frequency amplifiers use RC coupling.

blocks.text: Use one stage when gain is enough. Use a cascade when the required gain is higher than one stage can give with acceptable distortion.

Direct coupling joins the collector of one stage to the base of the next with a wire. No capacitor, so DC flows. The DC collector voltage of stage 1 is not the base voltage stage 2 needs. A level shifter or a second supply can fix this. Temperature drift and offset also pass on.

Transformer coupling uses a coil. The primary is in the collector, the secondary goes to the base. No DC path between primary and secondary; each side is biased separately. The turns ratio N<sub>2</sub>/N<sub>1</sub> changes impedance by (N<sub>2</sub>/N<sub>1</sub>)². It is bulky, costly and passes only a narrow band. RF and tuned amplifiers still use it.

items: Direct: used inside op-amps and ICs because large capacitors are hard to build on chip.
Transformer: used for impedance matching and isolation, not for DC.

sections.h3: Gain and bandwidth of a cascade

blocks.text: For stage voltage gains A<sub>1</sub>, A<sub>2</sub>, ..., the overall gain is the product.
A<sub>total</sub> = A<sub>1</sub> × A<sub>2</sub> × ...    and    A(dB) = 20 log₁₀ |A<sub>total</sub>|
blocks.where: A<sub>total</sub> is the overall voltage gain; A<sub>1</sub>, A<sub>2</sub> are stage voltage gains; |A<sub>total</sub>| is its magnitude; dB is decibels.

blocks.text: For n identical stages, each with lower cut-off f<sub>L</sub> and upper cut-off f<sub>H</sub>, the new cut-offs are below. Bandwidth B' is f<sub>H</sub>' − f<sub>L</sub>'.

blocks.where: f<sub>L</sub> and f<sub>H</sub> are the single-stage cut-offs in Hz; n is the number of identical stages; f<sub>L</sub>' and f<sub>H</sub>' are the cascaded cut-offs.

examples.question: Two identical RC-coupled stages each have midband gain 50, f<sub>L</sub> = 50 Hz and f<sub>H</sub> = 200 kHz. (a) Find the overall gain in dB. (b) Find the overall lower and upper cut-off frequencies and the new bandwidth.
steps: The two stage gains multiply: A<sub>total</sub> = A<sub>1</sub> × A<sub>2</sub> = 50 × 50 = 2500.
The gain in dB is A(dB) = 20 log₁₀(2500) = 20 × 3.39794 = 67.9588 dB, about 68 dB.
For n = 2 identical stages, the factor is r = √(2<sup>1/2</sup> − 1) = √(√2 − 1) = √0.414214 = 0.643594.
The new lower cut-off is f<sub>L</sub>' = 50 Hz / 0.643594 = 77.69 Hz, about 77.7 Hz.
The new upper cut-off is f<sub>H</sub>' = 200 kHz × 0.643594 = 128.72 kHz, about 128.7 kHz.
Convert f<sub>L</sub>' to kHz: 77.69 Hz = 0.07769 kHz. New bandwidth B' = 128.72 kHz − 0.07769 kHz = 128.64 kHz, about 128.6 kHz. The single-stage bandwidth was 199.95 kHz, so cascading narrowed it.
examples.answer: The overall gain is 2500, about 68 dB; the cut-offs are about 77.7 Hz and 128.7 kHz; the new bandwidth is about 128.6 kHz.
examples.check:
import math
A1 = 50.0
A2 = 50.0
At = A1 * A2
AdB = 20 * math.log10(At)
n = 2
r = math.sqrt(2 ** (1 / n) - 1)
fL = 50.0
fH = 200.0
fLp = fL / r
fHp = fH * r
Bp = fHp - fLp / 1000.0
print(round(At, 1))
print(round(AdB, 1))
print(round(fLp, 1))
print(round(fHp, 1))
print(round(Bp, 1))

traps: Multiplying dB values when cascading. In dB, gains add; as plain numbers, gains multiply.
Assuming cut-off frequencies stay the same. Identical cascaded stages raise gain but narrow the band.
Forgetting that the coupling capacitor blocks DC but not the AC signal. The next stage still needs its own bias.
Using turns ratio n instead of n² for transformer impedance matching.
Thinking direct coupling has no DC problem. It has no capacitor, but DC levels still shift and drift.

quiz.q: What does the coupling capacitor do in an RC-coupled amplifier?
quiz.a: It blocks DC between stages and passes the AC signal at midband.

quiz.q: Write the overall voltage gain of three stages with gains A1, A2 and A3.
Why does cascading identical stages reduce bandwidth?
quiz.a: Each stage has its own high-frequency roll-off. The combined response falls to the cut-off level sooner, so f<sub>H</sub> moves down. The low-frequency cut-off f<sub>L</sub> also moves up. Both the rise in f<sub>L</sub> and the fall in f<sub>H</sub> reduce the bandwidth.

quiz.q: Two stages have voltage gains 20 and 30. Find the overall gain in dB.
Three identical stages each have f_L = 40 Hz and f_H = 100 kHz. Find the cascaded cut-offs.
Why do op-amps use direct coupling even though it has drift?
quiz.a: Large coupling capacitors are hard to build on chip. Direct coupling allows DC gain, and differential stages plus level shifters control offset and drift.

quiz.q: Why is transformer coupling used in RF amplifiers but rarely in audio?
quiz.a: A transformer matches impedance and isolates DC, which suits narrowband RF. At audio it is bulky, costly and has a narrow band.

beyond: Not for the exam. In IC design, direct coupling with level shifters and current mirrors is standard; audio often uses RC or direct coupling; transformer coupling survives in RF tuned amplifiers and isolated gate drives.
